title: Knapsack and binary integer programming

problem.name: Knapsack and binary integer programming
problem.statement_latex:
\textbf{Zero-one knapsack.} Given positive integer weights $w_i$, nonnegative profits $p_i$ and capacity $W$, maximize $\sum_{i=1}^n p_ix_i$ subject to $x\in\{0,1\}^n$ and $\sum_{i=1}^n w_ix_i\le W$. The decision form also supplies a profit threshold. This models budgeted selection and resource allocation.

\entryalias{30}\textbf{Binary integer programming.} Given $A\in\mathbb Z^{d\times n}$ and $b\in\mathbb Z^d$, find $x\in\{0,1\}^n$ with $Ax\le b$, or decide infeasibility. A linear objective is handled through a profit threshold. The quantum regime of interest has fixed or slowly growing $d$ and binary-encoded coefficients; knapsack contributes capacity and profit-threshold inequalities.

The quantum bound uses coherent-memory time with bit-arithmetic costs; classical meet in the middle and capacity dynamic programming use RAM time, and Boolean encodings use bit complexity.

quantum.headline_latex: $\widetilde O(2^{n/3}n^d)$, Arvind--Schuler binary integer programming; $O^*(2^{n/3})$ for fixed $d$, including knapsack.
quantum.details_latex: Precomputed partial-sum vectors support coherent multidimensional range queries. The bound includes preprocessing and search; coefficient arithmetic contributes polynomial factors in bit length. For $d=o(n/\log n)$, the time is $2^{(1/3+o(1))n}$. Threshold search recovers the optimum with polynomial bit-length overhead. For knapsack, QuantumTreeGenerator additionally gives instance-dependent branch-and-bound estimates from classical solver trees. With $B$-bit coefficients, the reversible arithmetic has cost polynomial in $dn(B+\log n)$.

classical.headline_latex: $O^*(2^{n/2})$ for fixed $d$, meet in the middle with dominance searching; $O(nW)$ for knapsack, capacity dynamic programming.
classical.details_latex: The two half-assignment lists store partial-sum vectors and are matched by coordinatewise inequalities. Horowitz--Sahni knapsack removes dominated weight--profit pairs; capacity dynamic programming instead stores the best profit at each capacity. The smaller applicable bound supplies the comparison. A direct knapsack threshold circuit has size $O(n(B+\log n))$, retained when applying Boolean tensor contraction. If every integer-programming row has support at most fixed $r$, forbidden local assignments give fixed-width clauses on the original $n$ variables: polynomially many rows give $\operatorname{poly}(\text{input size})2^{O_r(n\log\log n/\sqrt{\log n})}$ time and polynomial space, while linearly many rows improve the exponent to $O_r(n/\sqrt{\log n})$.

strength.description_latex: The fixed-$d$, dense, large-coefficient comparison improves the exponential constant from $1/2$ to $1/3$, a polynomial speedup based on Grover search and amplitude amplification. Small capacities and bounded row support select the stated stronger classical bounds.

evidence.description_latex: Rigorous quantum bounds in the coherent-memory model, with partial evidence against the applicable classical algorithms. The separate branch-and-bound estimates depend on solver trees and implementation costs.

hardware.description_latex: Active registers contain $n$ assignment qubits and $d$ arithmetic accumulators; knapsack uses weight and profit registers of widths $O(\log W)$ and $O(\log\sum_i p_i)$, with reversible workspace. Exponential coherent range-search data and long coherent searches dominate useful fault-tolerant implementations.
